name: AI Programming with Python for Beginners
objectives: In Google Colab, explain how an AI model differs from rule-based code and import or install a Python library, with a correct one-sentence explanation and the library loading without errors

Given keywords and replies for a simple chatbot, use string tools and a dictionary to match a message to the right reply, matching regardless of capital letters and giving a default reply when nothing matches

Given your reply function, write a chat loop that ends when the user says bye and describe the limits of rule-based replies, with the loop exiting on bye and at least one example the rules cannot handle
Using the Hugging Face pipeline, load a pre-trained sentiment model, run it on a sentence and read its label and score, after reading the model card, with the label and score read correctly
Given a list of comments, run the model on every comment in a loop, count the labels and print a neat summary, with the counts matching the labels and scores rounded to two decimals

Given the model's results, flag results below a confidence threshold for a person to check and follow responsible AI habits, with every score under the threshold marked "check by hand" and no private data or keys in the notebook

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Python building blocks for AI

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI programming is, and setting up Colab
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what an AI model is and import a Python library in Colab.
This lesson builds toward: In Google Colab, you will explain how an AI model differs from rule-based code and import or install a Python library, with a correct one-sentence explanation and the library loading without errors.
Normal programming means you write every rule yourself: if the word is "hi", say "hello". AI programming means you use a model: a program that learned patterns from many examples, so it can handle cases you never wrote a rule for.
You rarely build a model from zero. You use a library: ready-made code someone else wrote and shared. In Python you load a library with import. Popular free AI libraries include Hugging Face Transformers (language models), scikit-learn (classic machine learning) and PyTorch (deep learning).
Google Colab already has many of these libraries. If one is missing, you install it in a cell with !pip install followed by its name. The ! tells Colab to run a system command instead of Python. Colab is free, but its computers are shared, so free resources are limited and can change.
Step by step:
- Open colab.research.google.com and make a new notebook.
- In a cell, type: import random
- Next line: print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
- Run it a few times and watch the answer change.
- If an import ever fails with "No module named", run !pip install <name> in a cell, then try again.
Words to know:
- AI model: a program that learned patterns from many examples and can make guesses on new data.
- Library: ready-made code you can load and use in your own program.
- import: the Python word that loads a library.
- pip: the tool that installs Python libraries.
- Rule-based: a program where a person wrote every rule by hand.
Official sources:
- Google Colab: Frequently Asked Questions
Try it now: In a new Colab notebook, import the random library and write a program that picks a random workout, snack or study topic from a list of five and prints it. Run it three times.
You can now explain the difference between rule-based code and an AI model, and import a library in Colab.

check.q: What is a library in Python?
options: A list of your saved notebooks
Ready-made code someone else wrote and shared
check.why: A library is shared, ready-made code you load with import.

check.q: You want to use scikit-learn but are not sure Colab has it. What would you try first?
options: Run import sklearn, and if it says "No module named", run !pip install scikit-learn
Type the library name into print()
check.why: Colab has many libraries already; install with !pip only if the import fails.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Strings and dictionaries: the brain of a simple chatbot
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use a dictionary to match keywords in a message to replies.
This lesson builds toward: Given keywords and replies for a simple chatbot, you will use string tools and a dictionary to match a message to the right reply, matching regardless of capital letters and giving a default reply when nothing matches.
AI programs work with a lot of text, so you need a few string tools. message.lower() makes text lower case, so "HELLO" and "hello" match. "hours" in message is True if the word appears anywhere in the message. message.split() breaks a sentence into a list of words.
A dictionary stores pairs: a key and a value, inside curly brackets. replies = {"hours": "We are open 9 to 5.", "price": "Prices are on our menu page."} You get a value with replies["hours"].
To build a chatbot brain, loop through the dictionary: for keyword, answer in replies.items(): if keyword in message: return answer. If nothing matches, return a default reply such as "Sorry, I do not know that yet."
Step by step:
- Make a dictionary of keywords and replies.
- Write a function reply(message).
- Inside, set message = message.lower().
- Loop through replies.items() and return the answer for the first keyword found.
- After the loop, return a default reply.
Words to know:
- String: text in Python.
- Dictionary: a set of key: value pairs in curly brackets.
- Key: the label you look up in a dictionary.
- Value: what is stored under a key.
- .items(): gives every key and value in a dictionary, for a loop.
Try it now: Write reply(message) for a pretend gym, library or food truck with at least four keywords (for example hours, price, location, contact). Test it with three messages, including one written in capital letters and one it should not understand.
You can now use string tools and a dictionary to match a message to the right reply.

check.q: What does "I need help now".split() give?
check.why: split() breaks a sentence into a list of words.

check.q: Your chatbot finds no keyword in the message. What would you have it do?
options: Print every reply in the dictionary
Return a default reply such as "Sorry, I do not know that yet."
check.why: A default reply handles messages that match no keyword.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making the chatbot talk, and seeing its limits
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your reply function in a loop that chats until the user says bye, and spot what rules cannot do.
This lesson builds toward: Given your reply function, you will write a chat loop that ends when the user says bye and describe the limits of rule-based replies, with the loop exiting on bye and at least one example the rules cannot handle.
A chatbot needs a loop: ask for a message, print the reply, and repeat. while True: repeats forever, so you add an exit: if the message is "bye", print a goodbye and use break to leave the loop.
Now test it like a real user would. Type "when do you open?" and your bot may fail, because you wrote "hours", not "open". Every new way of saying something needs a new rule. That is the main limit of rule-based programs.
This is exactly why AI models are useful: a language model learned from millions of sentences, so it can understand many ways of saying the same thing. In the next chapter you will use one.
Step by step:
- Start with while True:
- Inside, get message = input("You: ")
- If message.lower() == "bye", print a goodbye and break.
- Otherwise print("Bot:", reply(message)).
- Test with five different ways of asking the same question.
Words to know:
- while True: a loop that keeps going until something inside it stops it.
- break: leaves a loop right away.
- Limit: something a program cannot do well.
Try it now: Wrap your reply function from Lesson 2 in a chat loop that ends on "bye". Ask about hours in five different ways. Write down how many your bot understood, then add one rule to fix a miss.
You can now build a working rule-based chatbot loop and explain why rules alone are limited.

check.q: What does while True: do on its own?
options: Repeats forever until something like break stops it
Runs only if the user says bye
check.why: while True repeats forever, so you need an exit such as break.

check.q: Users keep typing "what time do you close?" and your rule-based bot fails. What would that tell you?
options: The bot has a typing error
Every new way of saying something needs a new rule, which is the limit of rule-based bots
Users should type in capital letters
check.why: Rule-based bots only match the rules you wrote; language models handle more ways of saying things.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Using a pre-trained AI model

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Loading a pre-trained model with Hugging Face
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Load a free sentiment model in Colab and use it on one sentence.
This lesson builds toward: Using the Hugging Face pipeline, you will load a pre-trained sentiment model, run it on a sentence and read its label and score, after reading the model card, with the label and score read correctly.
A pre-trained model is one someone already trained and shared, so you can use it right away. Hugging Face is a website that hosts thousands of free models, and its Transformers library loads them with one line.
The easiest tool is pipeline. You tell it the task and the model: classifier = pipeline("text-classification", model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"). This model reads English text and decides whether its mood (sentiment) is POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.
Use it like a function: classifier("The practice today was great!"). It returns a list with a dictionary inside, for example [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.99}]. The score is how sure the model is, from 0 to 1. The first run downloads the model, so it takes a little longer.
Always read a model's page (its "model card") before you use it: it says what the model was trained on, what it is for and its licence.
Step by step:
- In a new cell: from transformers import pipeline
- Create classifier = pipeline("text-classification", model="distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
- Run result = classifier("The practice today was great!")
- print(result[0]["label"], result[0]["score"])
- If transformers is missing, run !pip install transformers first.
Words to know:
- Pre-trained model: a model someone else already trained that you can use right away.
- Hugging Face: a website and set of libraries for sharing free AI models.
- pipeline: a Transformers tool that loads a model for a task in one line.
- Sentiment: the mood of a piece of text: positive or negative.
- Score: how sure the model is, from 0 to 1.
- Model card: the page that explains what a model does, its data and its licence.
Official sources:
- Hugging Face Transformers: Pipelines
- Hugging Face: distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model card
Try it now: Load the sentiment classifier and run it on three sentences you write: one clearly happy, one clearly upset, and one mixed like "The food was good but the wait was long." Print the label and score for each and note which one it was least sure about.
You can now load a pre-trained model with pipeline and read its label and score.

check.q: What does a model card tell you?
options: What the model was trained on, what it is for and its licence
check.why: Read the model card before using a model.

check.q: You run the classifier for the first time and it takes a while. What would you do?
options: Wait; the first run downloads the model
Change the label to POSITIVE by hand
check.why: The first run downloads the model, so it takes longer.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Running the model on many texts
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a loop to classify a list of comments and count the results.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of comments, you will run the model on every comment in a loop, count the labels and print a neat summary, with the counts matching the labels and scores rounded to two decimals.
Real programs handle many texts, not one. Put your comments in a list, then loop: for comment in comments: result = classifier(comment)[0]. You can also pass the whole list at once, classifier(comments), and get one result per comment back.
To summarize, keep counters: positive = 0 and negative = 0 before the loop, then add 1 to the right one inside it based on result["label"].
Round the score so it is easy to read: round(result["score"], 2) gives two decimal places. An f-string prints a neat line: print(f"{result['label']:8} {round(result['score'], 2)} {comment}").
Step by step:
- Put at least five comments in a list.
- Set positive = 0 and negative = 0.
- Loop through the comments and classify each one.
- Print the label, rounded score and comment.
- Add to the right counter, then print the totals after the loop.
Words to know:
- Counter: a variable that counts how many times something happened.
- round(): shortens a number to a set number of decimal places.
- Batch: a group of inputs handled together.
Try it now: Write six comments about a class, a team practice or a local shop. Classify them in a loop, print one neat line for each, and print how many were positive and how many negative.
You can now run an AI model over a list of texts and summarize the results with counters.

check.q: What does classifier(comments) give back when comments is a list?
options: One result for the whole list
check.why: Passing a list returns one result for each comment.

check.q: Inside your loop, result["label"] is "POSITIVE". What would you do with your counters?
check.why: Add 1 to the counter that matches the label.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking the AI and finishing the feedback sorter
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Flag low-confidence results for a person to check, and finish the feedback sorter.
This lesson builds toward: Given the model's results, you will flag results below a confidence threshold for a person to check and follow responsible AI habits, with every score under the threshold marked "check by hand" and no private data or keys in the notebook.
AI models make mistakes. This one only knows positive and negative, so neutral or mixed comments get forced into one of them. It can also miss sarcasm ("Great, another rainy game day.") and it was trained on English movie reviews, so slang or other languages may confuse it.
A good habit is a confidence threshold: if the score is below a number you choose, such as 0.80, the program says "check by hand" instead of trusting the label. A person makes the final call on anything that matters.
Use AI responsibly: do not run private messages through a tool without permission, do not paste passwords or API keys into a shared notebook, and tell people when a result came from AI.
You now have everything for the final task: a list, a model, a loop, an if with a threshold, counters and a clear printout.
Step by step:
- Choose a threshold, for example THRESHOLD = 0.80.
- Inside the loop, check: if result["score"] < THRESHOLD:
- Print "check by hand" next to those comments.
- Count positive and negative as before.
- Print the totals and how many need a human check.
Words to know:
- Threshold: a cut-off number you choose; results below it get special handling.
- Confidence: how sure a model is about its answer.
- Sarcasm: saying the opposite of what you mean, which models often miss.
- Human in the loop: a person reviews the AI's results before they are used.
Official sources:
- Hugging Face: distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model card
Try it now: Final task: build the feedback sorter. Use at least six comments, including one mixed and one sarcastic. Print each with its label and score, mark anything under 0.80 as "check by hand", and print the positive, negative and check-by-hand totals. Then read the flagged ones yourself and decide.
You can now build a working AI program in Python that sorts text, reports its results and hands unsure cases to a person.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Model loaded and used The model does not load, or no labels or scores are produced. The pre-trained sentiment model runs and gives a label and score for each comment. The notebook notes what the model card says it was trained on. Loop and printout Fewer than six comments, or comments are not each printed with label and score. At least six comments, each printed with its label and a rounded score. The printout is neatly lined up with an f-string. Counts The positive and negative counts are missing or wrong. Correct counts of positive and negative comments are printed. Also prints how many were marked "check by hand". Confidence threshold No threshold, or low scores are not flagged. Every score under 0.80 is marked "check by hand". Includes a sarcastic or mixed comment and explains why the model may get it wrong. Responsible use The notebook contains private messages without permission, or a password or API key. Only made-up or permitted comments, and no passwords or keys in the notebook. Adds a note saying the labels came from AI and a person checks the unsure ones. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why might this sentiment model get a neutral comment wrong?
options: It only knows positive and negative, so neutral comments are forced into one
check.why: The model has only two labels, so mixed or neutral comments get forced into one.

check.q: A friend wants you to run their private messages through your sorter. What would you do?
options: Run them without asking the people who wrote them
Paste your API key into the notebook to speed it up
Only use messages you have permission to use, and say the results came from AI
check.why: Responsible AI use means permission for private data and telling people when AI was used.
